declared.title: Feeling bad about being sad: The role of social expectancies in amplifying negative mood
declared.foundIn: docs/design/review-science.md (dossier du pilote, 2026-11-22) ; titre de mémoire de la session

population: adults in Australia and Japan (4 studies)

findings.text: Believing that others expect us not to feel sad goes with more negative emotion and less well-being, through judging ourselves negatively when we feel bad

support.sentence: The authors show that perceived social expectancies predict these differences in emotion and well-being both more consistently than-and independently of-personal expectancies and that they do so by promoting negative self-evaluation when experiencing negative emotion.

findings.text: In experiments, making people feel that others expect them not to be sad makes them feel worse after a negative event

support.sentence: We also find experimental evidence for the causal role of social expectancies in negative emotional responses to negative emotional events (Studies 3 and 4).

limits: it manipulates what others expect, not self-judgment directly: indirect for the book's claim
Australia and Japan; effects clearer in Australia
